title: Forces and Motion
blurb: The biggest chapter in the whole specification - about one fifth of every paper. Momentum, moments and the F = ma family come up relentlessly.
formulas: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
force × distance moved in the direction of the force
final velocity² = initial velocity² + 2 × acceleration × distance

items.q: State the formula linking momentum, mass and velocity.
a: momentum = mass × velocity
(p = m × v)
items.tip: Standard symbols are accepted, so p = mv is enough. Momentum is measured in kg m/s and it is a vector - it has a direction.

items.q: State the formula linking resultant (unbalanced) force, mass and acceleration.
a: force = mass × acceleration
(F = m × a)
items.tip: The word 'resultant' matters in the explanation questions: a body only accelerates if the forces on it are unbalanced.

items.q: State the formula linking moment, force and perpendicular distance from the pivot.
a: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
(M = F × d)
items.tip: Write the word 'perpendicular'. Distance must be measured at right angles to the line of action of the force.

a: For an object in equilibrium (balanced), the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot
equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that same pivot.
items.tip: Mark schemes accept this written mathematically, e.g. 'clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment'. You must mention the pivot.

items.q: State the principle of conservation of momentum / state what is meant by conservation of momentum.
items.rx: principle of conservation of momentum|meant by (the term )?conservation of momentum
a: In a closed system (no external forces acting), the total momentum before a collision or explosion
equals the total momentum after it - momentum is conserved.
items.tip: In the calculation that follows, choose a positive direction first and give anything moving the other way a minus sign. A negative answer just means it moves the opposite way.

items.q: Calculate the magnitude of force F acting on the beam / plank / arm.
a: Take moments about the pivot: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment;
substitute the known force × its perpendicular distance;
rearrange to make F the subject;
evaluate, and give the unit (N).
items.tip: Convert cm to m consistently, or keep everything in cm - just do not mix them. Marks are given for substitution and rearrangement even if the arithmetic slips.

items.q: Calculate the velocity of object A after the collision.
a: Total momentum before = total momentum after;
set up the equation: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂;
rearrange for the unknown velocity;
evaluate to 2 or more significant figures, with the direction stated.
items.tip: If the two objects stick together, the right-hand side becomes (m₁ + m₂) × v. Watch the signs - a rebound is negative.

items.q: Calculate the average force acting on the object during the collision.
a: Find the change in momentum: Δp = m × (v − u);
use force = change in momentum ÷ time;
evaluate, with the unit N.
items.tip: By Newton's third law, the force on A from B is equal in size and opposite in direction to the force on B from A.

items.q: State the magnitude and direction of the force that object A exerts on object B.
a: The magnitude is the same as the force B exerts on A;
the direction is opposite (Newton's third law).
items.tip: This is a free 2 marks if you spot that it is Newton's third law. The pair always acts on two different objects.

items.q: Use the velocity–time graph to calculate the acceleration / the distance travelled.
a: Acceleration = gradient of the graph = change in velocity ÷ time taken;
distance travelled = area under the graph;
split the area into triangles and rectangles and add them;
give the unit (m/s² for acceleration, m for distance).
items.tip: A horizontal line means constant velocity and zero acceleration. A negative gradient is deceleration.

items.q: Explain how the graph shows that the rubber band does not obey Hooke's law.
a: Hooke's law means extension is (directly) proportional to the force applied;
a proportional relationship gives a straight line through the origin;
this graph is curved / not a straight line, so extension is not proportional to force.
items.tip: Naming Hooke's law alone scores only 1 mark. You must say what the graph should have looked like and what it actually looks like.

items.q: Explain, in terms of the forces acting, why a falling object reaches terminal velocity.
a: Weight acts downwards and is constant;
at the start there is little or no drag, so the resultant force is large and the acceleration is large;
as speed increases, air resistance / drag increases;
so the resultant force decreases and the acceleration decreases;
eventually drag = weight, so the resultant force is zero;
acceleration is zero, so the object falls at a constant (terminal) velocity.
items.tip: This is a classic 6-marker. Follow the chain: forces → resultant → acceleration → speed, and never say 'gravity increases'.

items.q: Explain how a crumple zone / seat belt / air bag reduces the force on a passenger.
a: It increases the time taken for the passenger to stop;
the change in momentum is the same;
force = change in momentum ÷ time, so a longer time gives a smaller force (and smaller deceleration).
items.tip: Do not write 'it absorbs the shock'. The marks are for time, momentum change, and the formula.

items.q: State the factors that affect thinking distance and braking distance.
a: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance;
thinking distance increases with speed, alcohol or drugs, tiredness and distraction;
braking distance increases with speed, greater mass, wet or icy roads, and worn tyres or brakes.
items.tip: Multiple-choice versions of this appear constantly. Remember: anything about the car or the road affects only the braking distance; anything about the driver affects only the thinking distance.

items.q: Calculate the work done / show that the work done is about X J.
a: work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force;
substitute, using only the component of distance along the force;
evaluate and give the unit (J).
items.tip: In a 'show that' question you must still write out the full working and state a more precise answer than the one given.
